content: The influenza virus strains B/Malaysia/2506/2004 and B/Ohio/1/2005 belong to the B/Victoria/2/87 lineage. 2007 Influenza Season (Southern Hemisphere) The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended the following composition for influenza virus vaccines for the 2006 Southern Hemisphere influenza season on September 20, 2006: An A/New Caledonia/20/99 (H1N1)-like virus. An A/Wisconsin/67/2005 (H3N2)-like virus. At the time, A/Wisconsin/67/2005 and A/Hiroshima/52/2005 were used. A B/Malaysia/2506/2004-like virus. 2007–2008 Influenza Season (Northern Hemisphere) The WHO recommended the following composition for influenza virus vaccines for the 2007–2008 Northern Hemisphere influenza season on February 14, 2007: An A/Solomon Islands/3/2006 (H1N1)-like virus. An A/Wisconsin/67/2005 (H3N2)-like virus. At the time, A/Wisconsin/67/2005 (H3N2) and A/Hiroshima/52/2005 were used. A B/Malaysia/2506/2004-like virus. 2008 Influenza Season (Southern Hemisphere) The WHO recommended the following composition for influenza virus vaccines for the 2008 Southern Hemisphere influenza season on September 17–19, 2007: An A/Solomon Islands/3/2006 (H1N1)-like virus. An A/Brisbane/10/2007 (H3N2)-like virus. A B/Florida/4/2006-like virus. Veterinary Influenza Vaccination Vaccination in veterinary medicine aims to achieve four primary goals: 1. Protection from clinical disease. 2. Protection from infection with virulent virus strains. 3. Prevention of virus shedding. 4. Serological differentiation between infected and vaccinated animals (the DIVA principle). In the context of influenza vaccination, no commercially available or experimentally tested vaccines have yet been shown to meet all these criteria. Horses Horses infected with equine influenza may exhibit symptoms such as fever, a dry hacking cough, nasal discharge, depression, and reluctance to eat or drink. Recovery typically occurs within 2–3 weeks. Vaccination schedules for horses generally involve a primary course of two doses administered 3–6 weeks apart, followed by booster doses at 6–12 month intervals. However, in high-risk situations, more frequent administration may be necessary to maintain protective antibody levels. Poultry Poultry vaccines for avian influenza are produced at a lower cost and are not filtered or purified to the same standards as human vaccines. These vaccines often contain whole virus particles rather than just hemagglutinin, as is common in human flu vaccines. Purification to human standards is significantly more expensive than producing unpurified vaccines from eggs, and there is no market for such costly veterinary vaccines. Poultry vaccines are adjuvanted with mineral oil, which induces a strong immune response but can cause inflammation and abscesses. Accidental self-injection by poultry vaccinators has resulted in painful swelling, and in some cases, loss of digits. The effectiveness of poultry vaccines may be limited, as they are often only loosely related to circulating flu strains. For example, some vaccines contain an H5N2 strain isolated in Mexico years ago. According to Dr. Cardona, a vaccine that is only 85% related to the circulating strain may provide some protection, but even a 99% match may not be sufficient. Poultry vaccines are designed to protect birds for their short lifespan (approximately six weeks) before they are processed for consumption. Pigs Swine influenza virus (SIV) vaccines are widely used in the swine industry in Europe and North America. Most commercial swine flu vaccines include H1N1 and H3N2 SIV strains. However, the evolution of the virus has led to inconsistent responses to traditional vaccines. Standard commercial vaccines are effective when the virus strains are sufficiently matched to provide cross-protection. In more challenging cases, custom (autogenous) vaccines are developed using specific virus isolates. For example, the H3N2 strain of SIV, first identified in the U.S. in 1998, has caused significant production losses in the swine industry. Symptoms include abortion storms, sows refusing to eat for 2–3 days, and fevers up to 106°F. Mortality in naïve herds can reach as high as 15%. Research on Avian Influenza Researchers led by Nicholas Savill at the University of Edinburgh used mathematical models to simulate the spread of H5N1 avian influenza. They concluded that at least 95% of birds need to be protected to prevent silent virus transmission. In practice, achieving protection for more than 90% of a flock is challenging, and the protection levels provided by vaccines are often much lower.
